title: Harmful speech
hook: speech that harms, even when it's true

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was achrayut, and your line: carry your share. Today a new stretch begins, on speech, starting with the tongue.

Did you hear about Dan? He got let go. Apparently he'd been missing deadlines for months. Two people at a coffee machine. Every word is true. Nobody is lying, nobody is shouting, and nobody would call it cruel. It's just news, passed along with a little lift in the voice. Dan isn't there. He'll never know this conversation happened. And yet Jewish tradition has a name for that sentence, and it treats it as a serious wrong.
screen: `EVERY WORD IS TRUE.` → `DAN ISN'T THERE.` → `THE SENTENCE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Lashon hara. Literally, the evil tongue: speech that harms, even when it's true. You got a first glimpse of it long ago, with tzara'at, the skin affliction read as speech made visible. Turn it four ways. First, the true part. Saying something false about a person is a different wrong, and it gets its own name later this week. Lashon hara is about true things: a failure, a weakness, an embarrassing story, told in a way that lowers someone. Accurate isn't the same as kind. Second, the story. In Numbers, Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses. God's anger burns, and Miriam is struck with a skin disease and shut outside the camp for seven days, while the whole people waits for her. Deuteronomy later says to remember what God did to Miriam on the way out of Egypt, and tradition reads that as a warning about speech. Third, the three it wounds. The Talmud, in tractate Arakhin, says lashon hara kills three: the one who speaks it, the one who hears it, and the one it's about. The speaker gets smaller. The listener can't unhear it. And the one it's about pays for a conversation they weren't in. Fourth, the exception. Some harmful truth may be spoken when it's needed to protect someone, like warning a friend about a business partner who cheats. The rules are careful, and the purpose has to be help, not entertainment. That's the line: does this sentence protect someone, or just make a good story?
screen: `TRUE, AND STILL HARMFUL.` · `REMEMBER WHAT GOD DID TO MIRIAM.` · `IT KILLS THREE.` · `PROTECTION, NOT ENTERTAINMENT.` · then, large: `NO GOSSIP.`

segments.voice: Picture where gossip usually finds you: a group chat, a lunch table, a family dinner, the moment someone's name comes up and the story starts to lean. Find an easy sentence for that moment, like I don't really know the whole story, or let's talk about something else, and rehearse it once in your head. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words.
Lashon hara. The evil tongue: true words about someone that lower them, when no one needs protecting. Today's word.
Your line: no gossip. A true word can still be a heavy one. Day done.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the laws of guarding speech a little each day, and some communities and schools hold days or hours set aside for speaking no lashon hara at all.

chat.says: But everything I said about him is true. How can that be gossip?
options: Lashon hara is true speech that lowers someone; being accurate doesn't make it kind.
It's only gossip if you exaggerate; plain facts about people are always fine to share.
It's only harmful if the person finds out what was said about them.
